back: Authentication proves who the caller is; authorization decides what that caller may do. 401 means not authenticated, 403 means authenticated but not allowed.

front: Server-side session: main strength and main cost?
back: Strength: instant logout and live permissions (delete the record). Cost: a store lookup on every request, so the store sits on the critical path.

front: Three cookie flags for a session cookie?
back: HttpOnly (no JavaScript access), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite=Lax or Strict (limits cross-site sending).
The browser holds only an HttpOnly session cookie; a server-side component holds the OAuth tokens and attaches them to API calls. Tokens never reach browser JavaScript.
Delegated authorization: an app gets an access token to call an API on a user's behalf without ever seeing the user's password.
The client sends SHA-256(code_verifier) as code_challenge on /authorize, then must present the raw code_verifier at /token. A stolen code is useless without the verifier.

front: Which OAuth grants does RFC 9700 rule out?
back: Implicit (tokens in the browser URL) and resource owner password credentials (the app collects the password). Use authorization code + PKCE instead.

front: Client credentials grant: when and what's missing?
back: Machine-to-machine calls with no user. The client authenticates as itself; no refresh token is issued because it can simply request a new token.
ID token (OIDC): a JWT for the client saying who logged in. Access token (OAuth): a credential for the API. Never send an ID token to an API.

front: Which ID token claims must a client check?
back: iss equals the expected issuer, aud contains its client ID, exp not passed, nonce matches what it sent. Key users by iss + sub, not email.

front: Is a signed JWT's payload secret?
back: No. It is base64url-encoded, so anyone holding the token can read it. Signing provides integrity, not confidentiality.
HS256 uses one shared secret, so every verifier can also mint tokens. RS256 and ES256 sign with a private key and verify with a public key published in a JWKS.
A server expecting RS256 accepts an HS256 token and uses its RSA public key as the HMAC secret, so anyone with the public key can forge tokens. Fix: pin algorithms on the verifier.
Validity comes from the signature and exp, not a database row, so verifiers have nothing to consult. A copied token works until exp unless you add state back.

front: Refresh token rotation with reuse detection?
back: Each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If an old one is presented again, the server revokes the whole token family.

front: How big is a jti denylist?
back: Entries live only until exp. 1M logouts/day with a 15-minute TTL means about 1,000,000 / 96 = 10,400 live entries.
